utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Martinovic and Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I asked for two minutes, or even less, to address you because I feel it is necessary for me to apologise to the Trial Chamber, and to my learned friends, the Prosecutors, for the possible omissions I made yesterday. I didn't do it intentionally. I didn't do it on purpose. I didn't do it in order to create difficulties to my learned friends or to this distinguished Trial Chamber. I did this only because I was guided by the primary concern of not harming my client in any way. I know that I did not have translations into the English language. We did our very best. We found a certified translator, and we have got everything this morning. We have the letter translated and the video transcript. I kindly ask my learned friends to accept my apology and to realise that it was all done with the best of intentions without any ill intentions. Please accept my apology. And now I would like to tender all the copies, all the copies of the translation of the videotape transcript, and also the letter which was only in the Croatian language. Thank you. Your Honours, in order to assist you and in order to assist my learned friends, if they don't mind, I also made an effort to translate the "Glossary of Religious Terms" which was published in Sarajevo in 1999, and it was published by the Religious Council of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If my colleagues do not mind, and if they are not challenging this, I would like to hand this out over -- I would like to hand this out now as well, because it's going to make things much easier when certain terms are referred to in documents, in this videotape and videotapes that may come in the future. If my learned friends from the OTP do not mind, if they do not object to this, I am going to hand in copies. I am going to ask the witness about this book, too, just one question. It's a public book. I mean it was published. So I'm doing this only to assist you, Your Honours, and my learned friends of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters get a copy, please. Interpreters' note: Could the interpreters please get these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have this handed in immediately. Is that all right? Could I please hear the response of my learned friend from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, could I hear your initial response to all those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, having just received them, I'm not in a position to make any significant response because I've never seen some of these documents before. We will take a look at them and get back to the Chamber as soon as we've had a chance to study them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Shall we go with the witness at this moment? No? Mr. Krsnik, are we going to have the witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [no translation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, it may assist us to make -- to answer the Chamber's questions if we could obtain a bit more information. Perhaps it's on here, and again having just received it just a couple of minutes ago, is this -- is the title of the book, "Glossary of Religious Terms"? And what is the source of the book? What is the publisher? And who authored it? Could we possibly get that information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. That is the title of the book. I have the original here in the Croatian. The book is called, "A Glossary of Religious Terms." It was published by The Inter-religious Council of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, this was translated by the certified translators of this Tribunal, so that is this additional piece of information. It's quite a big book, but we only wanted to have the most important terms translated in order to facilitate our work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I have to remind you that you are still under the solemn declaration. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yesterday we viewed the tape. Since we have -- we all have the transcript now, could we have it again but with the sound track on?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they did not get a transcript; therefore it cannot be interpreted. We are sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you provide a transcript to the interpreters? Mr. Krsnik? I think the interpreters also need the transcript of this videotape, if you want to have it translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. We have provided all of this to the lady from the Registry. We gave all our copies to her.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have just received copies. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible to -- for us to see only parts of this video?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have made an abbreviated version, Your Honour. I gave it to the registrar and to the Prosecutors. This is a longer version, but I did this in order to save time. I'm going to ask the technical booth to play only the first part, which is perhaps of the greatest interest, and my questions will be derived from that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's play the videotape again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the technical booth to fast-forward the beginning, please. Can we start from here, please. Perhaps a bit more, and could you pause then, please. From here, please. Could we start playing it at normal speed from here, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Mr. General, the soldiers from the 4th Muslim Light Brigade are ready for your ... Soldiers and officers salute to the father land, salute. Tekbir. Alahu egber. Tekbir. Alahu egber. Tekbir. Alahu egber. Tekbir. Alahu egber. [Arabic phrase] Allah wo lala, Mohamed dires a lala, mahas dires a lala, Allah do hala, Mohamed dires a lala [phoen]. To the left, to welcome the war banner. Welcome to all of those who have come to Jablanica, to a free Jablanica, to join this big celebration of lining up the 4th Muslim Light Brigade of the 4th Corps of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thank you all, all of those who have come to stand before the best men of this corps. Thank you to all who have come to share with us this great joy and this truly solemn moment. Salem alejkum. I will start with Sura verse from the Koran. Allah truly loves those who fight on his path, and they are like a solid construction, meaning that they are unbreakable, that they are impenetrable. Following these words from the Koran, only one dawning on the battlefield on Allah's path is better than the world or all that is in it, or as it says in the second part, it is better to have ibadet for -- than 60 years. And following this Koran teaching, the 4th Muslim Light Brigade was formed and became stronger and is still growing in strength and still operates in this area. I'm sure that you will obey those orders and regulations in a disciplined manner and that you will remain an example of what an army should be like and what the army's elite units should be like. It gives me particular pleasure to introduce the Herzegovina Mufti, Hadji Seid Efendi Smajkic, who will take the floor. Dear and honoured brothers, dear soldiers, dear officers, it is my great honour in this mubarek month of Ramadan, which is the symbol of our greatest victories of Muslims through history, to greet and extend my selamet to our dear soldiers who insallah will carry the greatness of our religion and the glory of our state of Bosnia-Herzegovina through this area for which they will fight as they have shown in their battle so far. I invite the emir of the 7th Muslim Glorious Mountain Brigade, Mahmut Efendija Karalic, to take the floor, please. Dear lads, we did not find it difficult to come this far and meet you today at this celebration of yours since we are bound by the same goals and duties. The first and basic aim is the protection of din and Islam in these areas; secondly, the protection of the honour and dignity of the Muslim people and our own homes. We know that we are a small nation, that we are bare-handed, if you like, that we are a people without a military tradition in this area, because there were very few of our people, our officers, in the former JNA, who could progress. Why? Now we find out why. Both the 7th Muslim Glorious Brigade and the 4th Muslim Light Brigade and all other Muslim brigades go into battle with those aims. They go to battle, their basic weapons being the prayer rug and prayer and only then the things they have. That is why success is inshalah inevitable. However, brothers, the other units of other army are all of -- consisting of Muslim soldiers. They all have shehadet, the truth in their hearts. Something that somebody said previously, someone sends more and someone less, and in that sense there is less success, but I hope that to us that we have no alternative here in Bosnia. Unless we return to an our traditions and unless we gain military strength, we cannot survive in these areas. In order to be militarily strong, we must return to our source, to our tradition, religion and culture. On that note, I congratulate you and my wish is that Allah may help you in your future battles. Dear delegates of the Bosniak Muslim people, I personally believe that for us the time that we are ashamed of what we are and where we come from has long passed; therefore, as soon as possible, we realise who and what we are, what generation we are, what is our spirit, then I'm sure that we will faster overcome the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the crisis among the Muslim Bosniak people. Therefore, soldiers, officers, do not be ashamed of what you really are, and we are, to put it simply, Bosniak Muslims. We are fighting for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We are fighting for the Bosniak Muslim people . We have told you this a thousand times, that in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina there is room for all, but we have also told you that there is no room in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina for those by name and surname regardless of the fact that they are Bosniak Muslims if they do not consider the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Bosnian Muslim people as their own. Therefore, for us they are traitors, and we have during this battle, this revolutionary battle, and patriotic way in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Bosniak Muslim people met with such individuals. The president of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. In the name of Allah, merciful and gracious, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 4th Corps, the 4th Muslim Light Brigade. Honourable Mr. President, it is human, military and patriotic that from this solemn position, this solemn lining up of our brigade, we address you in this way. This historic moment, this formation before us, obliges us for something like this, because we consider you as part of this brigade. Above all, a man who, through his effort, contributed that today on the 10th Ramadan of 14, 15, on the 9th February 1995, the 4th Muslim Light Brigade with their heads held high proudly stands here before us, its people. We, the Mujahedin of the 4th Muslim Light Brigade, together with all other patriots of our state, from the first day of aggression against our country, we stood up to the tormentor and enemy with our arms and our lives, and now for three years we have been defending, liberating our country, protecting our people from total destruction. Our Mujahedin have spilled their blood on many a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The blood of our shehids in the -- tinted both Butmir and Kijevo and Kotorac and Ljubina and Bijela Ljeska and Bjeljevice and Ivan. Our state is the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this is the zone of responsibility of our brigade. A large number of our Mujahedin have been forced from their homes. They have lost their dearest. They were humiliated and mistreated. Our struggle is a struggle for our return to our homes but also a return for all of those Bosniak Muslims who have been scattered around the world by the enemy. Our struggle is a struggle for the dignity of the Muslim people, for its freedom, its religion, our only homeland, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. President, rest assured that the gazie of the 4th Muslim Light Brigade know nothing else but to march forward and only forward with the name of Allah dzelasunum on their lips and the rifles in their hands, because we thank -- thanks be to Allah dzelasunum have the will and kuhvet to continue to fight for our homeland and our people and that we will never think of surrender and give up on our honourable heroic fight. We want to let you know, Mr. President, that we know that battle ask our only destiny and only through battle can we return the dignity to our people and freedom to our country. We are, therefore, not afraid of death and the honourable path of Allah and we will never surrender. Know this: As long as there are mujahedin of our brigade, while there are mujahids throughout our state the Bosnia and Herzegovina, as long as there are soldiers of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the battle continues. We are ready for it and impatiently waiting for the resumption of military activities for the final liberation of our country. Your efforts and the efforts of your associates, like the current battle of the 5th Corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, are a higher imperative at this moment. With faith in the dear Allah dzelasunum, we are following the path of freedom, justice and prosperity. We ask the sublime Allah dzelasunum to help us in the battle for freedom for Bosnia-Herzegovina and to give you health and the strength to persevere along the paths of truth. Victory or death, [Arabic phrase] Al salam ou alaykum el ekmitutam el bekiatum [phoen]. Attention: Line up right. Attention: To salute the war banner, turn your eyes right. Eyes left. All of these are soldiers who have in the past three-year war grown into capable officers with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They have left many battles behind. They keep going on with the help of Allah. Now we are introducing the 1st Squad of the 3rd Infantry Company who in the marching competition notice 4th Corps zone of responsibility have won the first prize. Get up army. It is sabah. It is prayer time. We are going to the camps and then to the graves. We are all the Jihad army. Victory is sweet. We will kill the enemy. Less Chetniks will fall. All will be volunteers. Our guys will break you. Let them know this too. We'll kill. Allah cursed him. Passing by is the 1st Infantry Company headed by Mujo Vrkic of the 4th Light Brigade. It is the 1st Infantry Company headed by Mujo Vrkic, the 1st Infantry Company of the 4th Light Brigade. The 2nd Infantry Company, headed by its commander, Saldo Spago. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Salute to the left. The 3rd Infantry Company, headed by its commander, Muhamed Hodzic. These are mostly lads who finished their training in the recruit teaching centre, training centre, of the 4th Corps of the army of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Bradina. The 4th Infantry Company, headed by its commander, Mehmed Lijevo. The 5th Infantry Company, headed by its commander, Hamdija Jelovac. This is the famous MOS from Mostar who defended Mostar in Santic Street and contributed to the survival of the Bosniak Muslim people in the Mostar area. I now invite the choirs from Konjic, Jablanica, and Mostar to perform an appropriate art and cultural programme prepared for this celebration, the celebration of the 4th Muslim Light Brigade. Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think this is enough, Your Honours. I do not think that the rest of the tape is relevant. May I now cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: To begin with, good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you some questions, and I should like to ask you to help us distinguish certain terms. To begin with, do you know about this "Glossary of Religious Terms" which was issued by the Inter-Religious Council of Bosnia-Herzegovina in '92?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what does the word --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you have it there, right, tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, not all terms are here. We do not know what is "shekhadet" in the heart?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means carry within one faith in God.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what does "mujahid" mean?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combatants, fighters. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Nothing else. I see. And what does "jihad" mean?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would take a longer explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell us in a few words, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and witness pause between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Jihad" both as a term and the substance of this word means struggle, struggle for the state, for the survival of the state, the struggle for one's faith and its survival, the struggle for the survival and preservation of life. It is struggle for the preservation of property and struggle for the preservation of honour, of honour and dignity. These five factors. These are in the briefest possible terms. If any one of these are threatened, then the struggle becomes a separate condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is it the struggle on Allah's path, or you say that we, mujahid, we liberate Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you mean also liberation for Serbs and Croats, too? Or is the jihad only the struggle along the Allah's path?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It need not be. Jihad doesn't have only this religious aspect. I've just listed you five basic factors for which one needs to fight. And if you fight for any one of these factors, when they are in danger, then this is the -- then this is jihad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This word -- another word is often mentioned. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I make another explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another explanation regarding Jihad which goes beyond war and which is considered the strongest Jihad of all, that is, stronger participation in offensive operations, is the struggle. That is how Islam defines it: It is the struggle with one's own negative instincts with one's own animal passion. It is the struggle to have the noble, the generous side of the human being win.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now my last question: If one says that we are off on a jihad for the state -- for instance, in Croatia -- for instance, Muslims in the Republic of Croatia, in the state of Croatia, it has nothing to do with other Muslims, or does it? Because this is jihad for Croatia only. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell me, please, did you or this army of Bosnia-Herzegovina receive support from soldiers or mujahid? We have just heard that that word means "combatants" and nothing else but, even though there is another interpretation, that they are God's warriors, that they are holy warriors. Would you agree with that, because there is such interpretation?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, depends on how you interpret the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise. You do not have this glossary before you, but may I read out to you what the glossary says about the "mujahid." "Mujahid," it says, is a person who makes a spiritual, intellectual, or physical effort to promote good, fight against evil - and I can't really see - and defend the rights of every man to practice Islam freely with no hinderance. Colloquially, this is a warrior on God's path. So that is it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So did the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina receive assistance from any other countries, from any foreign countries, both in terms of troops, that is, mujahids, and financial support?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was supported financially and with a small number of combatants, very limited number, as far as I know. I, of course, am not the most competent person to speak about that. I'm simply voicing my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I asked you that because you said yesterday that the HVO was receiving foreign support and that was why the aggression took place. Now, if the BH army was also supported from outside by foreign combatants, does it mean that Iran or Iraq committed an aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that question is out of place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But you forced me to ask this question because that is what you said yesterday. I simply tried to draw a parallel. I apologise. I was not trying to ask you any "out of place" questions. What I meant was support to the HVO from Croatia, from the Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, that is a different state, just as the combatants who joined your army, the BH army, came from other states. They did not come from the Bosnia state. They came from other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So my question is perfectly logical. But well, never mind.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But people, members of foreign legions from all over, joined the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, now, you've just confirmed what I'm trying to say. It was a conflict within Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it was not a conflict within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Fine. Tell me, please, now that we've seen these images, I do not know -- and perhaps I missed it because the copy is not good. But the other day when I watched it at home, I did not see the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina anywhere. All I saw were the banners which the soldiers had. Yes, I think that on the days, I believe -- yes, I think was this flag, if I am correct. But the troops never had the flags of Bosnia-Herzegovina; they are all flags -- if I understand it well, and you will help me, they all had inscriptions from Koran. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a manifestation. It is a sentence which says that there is no God but God, no Allah but Allah. And excuse me, I did spot the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And don't forget, after all, that we watched the march of the Muslim Brigade. I mean, it is called the Muslim Brigade. Other units, other units, units which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, sorry to interrupt, but the transcript is amiss. Again, it has statements from counsel being attributed to the witness, and I think in some potentially important respects. For instance, it has attributed to the witness's answer that the troops never had the flags of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm confident that this witness did not say that, but again, we're having problems with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have problems that sometimes the questions and answers mingle together. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- you could clear it up for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I said here on this videotape. I did not go beyond videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Remember that I asked you that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness confirms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the witness said that he thought he had seen the flag.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see that flag, but I wish to remind you that this is the 4th Muslim Brigade and these are its symbols.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, this Mr. Halilovic who was all in black, he is an imam or hodza; he is a cleric, isn't he, if I may translate it?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an imam or hodza, but he quit the service in the Islamic community and joined the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And which year is it that he became an active soldier?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think from the very beginning of the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, because he is a man from Zepa, from the Drina Valley and so on and so forth, where people were victimised. I know it because at that time, he worked under me. And he said he wanted to quit the religious service and devote himself to the defence of the state. So he became a professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I asked you that because yesterday, when I asked you if from your area, from the territory under your jurisdiction, there were any imams or hodzas in the army, and your answer was yes. But you said today you did not say that he became active.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is my full answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I see. Tell me, is the duty of a hodza or imam compatible with such a commitment, or is it a normal thing in Islam?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one couldn't do both things simultaneously, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All right, all right. We get the point. And tell us, Efendi Karavelic, is he a hodza? -- that is, that other gentleman from the 7th Muslim Brigade, the one with the beard who delivered the speech.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Karalic, Efendi Karalic, is he a hodza, too?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a medresa teacher, which is a secondary religious school in Sarajevo. And in the early days of the aggression of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he also quit that service and joined actively the struggle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: As far as we heard it, there was no speech between them - and you told us there was - between 4th light and all the other units, 4th and the 7th Brigade. That is, all members of the Muslim army, they are all on the days, you all carry shekhadet in your heart, and so on and so forth. So one is emir, another one is a brigade commander, a commander. He even calls traitors those Muslims who do not accept such an army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the name of such one is Drekovic. The commander of the 4th Corps said that those who did not accept such army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were traitors.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think you are interpreting it right, sir, because if you want an explanation, the men arrived from the area of the 5th Corps from Krajina where some dissident forces, Bosniak forces, were cooperating with the enemies of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is what he had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right. Never mind. Tell me, did all the Muslims in Herzegovina agree with such an army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Will you answer this question, first: Did all the Muslims agree with such an army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in late '92 and early '93 at the time of its formation? And it says here that they are all combatants of the Grija war [phoen]. This is '95. So that is all combatants date back to '92, and all their officers, too.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wartime events and the circumstances under which these combatants matured made of them what they are. At the outset, no doubt on many occasions, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was quite different from the one that we just saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My question is: Did all the Muslims in Herzegovina embrace such an army? That was my question. And you gave me a different answer. So will you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I don't understand what that question means. Agreed with such an army? Such an army as what? That there was an armed Muslim force defending? What is "such an army"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I have the same doubts, Mr. Scott. Maybe you could rephrase the question to make your question more clear to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question will be very clear. I thought it was clear already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did all the Muslims in Herzegovina agree with the formation of a religious army, the army of the Muslim people rather than the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the army of one party? Is my question now clear? And you can answer whatever you think is right.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they did not because the circumstances were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, didn't the commander of the general staff of Armija Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sefer Halilovic, quit the army sometime I believe end of May '93 because he disagreed with those principles that I mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. Mr. Halilovic is in the Hague, so it is best to ask him. He will know the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one more question. Mostar MOS, M-O-S, was mentioned here. Can you tell us, what is MOS?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a small unit which made part of the Mostar Brigade. I think it is a company, a company strong group of guys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me, what does the acronym "MOS" mean?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, are you aware that your highest religious leader, reis-ul-ulema Mustafa Ceric, on the 26th of May, '93, on Radio Sarajevo proclaimed a jihad saying the holy war of Islam against the infidels. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you ever make any statements on television?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And in the sense of the imperial role of the Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Fine. If you don't remember, you don't.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. During the war, many correspondents came. When did they say what? It is possible that, in that sense, in view of the role of the Catholic church, it is possible that I did say something, but now I simply couldn't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My question is: Did you, with the money that you received from the SDA, form a unit made of refugees from Gacko and Nevesinje and headed it personally, a unit which was called Sargani?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received any money from the SDA, nor was I a part of Sargani. I have already said that I did not participate in any units. I was simply a man exercising, discharging, this office, a man of my profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you aware of an independent unit called The Muslim Forces?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You need to say something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That's its name, The Muslim Forces. It's an independent unit, The Muslim Forces.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, did it operate in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In Mostar, and under your patronage. If you know about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it, fine; if you don't, you don't. As a matter of fact, you established a commission that had to deal with how many weapons you had?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This unit grew into it. There were a few young men there who wanted to establish a unit of that kind and it grew into MOS. That is MOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Oh, I see. That is MOS. And now, could you please tell me whether you were in Mostar from April until June 1992, that is to say, at the time of the Chetnik aggression?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You didn't go anywhere from Mostar? All that time, throughout that three-month period?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From April until the liberation of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go anywhere, except to Split or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go anywhere. I'm surprised. How do you come up with all these things?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking. I'm asking. I'm asking whether you went anywhere, and you say you didn't go anywhere, and I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell me, your muftiluk was actually stationed in the students' dormitory. Were there Kandis [phoen] and were Dzuma and Bajram Namaz celebrated there at that time? I'm talking about 1992 and Bishop Peric and everything, remember. Were conditions created for your religious services? Was it possible for you to carry out your religious services? Did anybody ever stop you from doing that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the students' dormitory, we had an adapted gym. The gym was actually adapted into a praying area, and we were unhindered. However, people who went to the mosques in Balinovac and Pijesak, when it was Bajram, had some unpleasant things happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know that Catholic priests also had problems when they went to conduct religious services in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Vukcic, the parish priest, who on the evening of the 8th of May, 1993, who had something happen to him? Actually, the Muslim forces barged into his house, which was by his church, and detained him in East Mostar. So that happened on the evening of the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of this case. I am --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, go ahead, go ahead. I'm not going to stop you. Please say whatever you feel you should say.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not on the 8th of May. It was when the Croatian offensive started, on the 9th of May. So the soldiers of the army crossed the Bulevar line and in that house where the Bishop's Caritas was -- I mean they came to that house, and they took Mr. Vukcic, and they took him with them in order to save his life. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Oh, very well.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not in any kind of detention or prison. He was staying with a very respectable man of ours, at his home, at this respectable man's home, until conditions were right for his return to the west part. That is what I know, and that is what is certainly the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please explain this to us? The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina crosses the line of the Bulevar, gets to West Mostar - all of that is West Mostar, by the way - to save his life from whom? I mean, a Catholic parish priest, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is trying to save a Catholic priest's life, from whom?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to give you accurate information so that you know. From the 9th of May onwards, there were large-scale attacks against the western part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do not interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But please answer my question. My question is very simple. Who were they saving his life from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you have to be very patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I am patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to be very patient. Let the witness answer the question first. Yes, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the offensive that was launched by the Croatian side, the units clashed at the Bulevar and Mr. Vukcic happened to be in that whirlpool. And now our units, in order to protect his life, and in the meantime, the Croat forces were advancing and they pushed back the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they took with them Mr. Vukcic, and they provided accommodation for him, lodgings. So I assure you, I give you my word of honour, that he was not in any kind of detention or prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell me, this statement that he gave to Radio Mostar, I mean when he was in detention, again, are you going to give us your word of honour that this was voluntary, this, what was done by this priest, Vukcic?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Oh, you didn't hear it? And now, tell me --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In your letter to Bishop Peric, you are talking about this statement given to Radio Mostar, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall every little detail. It is quite understandable. But I know the event itself. I can tell you about it from the beginning until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yesterday you said that it was only Muslims who were waiting in lines for aid at Caritas and that Croats awaited it at home, at their homes. Correct me if I'm wrong, but you did say something to that effect, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say it that way. I did say that particularly at the beginning, from April onwards, that there were people belonging to all ethnic groups but that most of them were Muslims. However, since that situation later changed, according to the concepts of leaders and politicians, people who were waiting in front of the church were mostly Muslims. And later, considerably later, we can say from January 1993 onwards, Croats or Catholics received parcels at their home addresses - I know that for sure - and the Muslims remained standing there, hanging out in front of the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you do not know that Muslims came by name and surname and that there were lists for every month, and not a single list was shorter than 3.000 names, and they would come directly to Caritas or they would have parcels sent to their homes because there was no need to wait for aid?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that most people had to ask for this and to wait in long lines in front of Caritas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know a saying from those days, that everybody was saying in Mostar, both the Muslims and the Croats, "The HVO is defending us, and Caritas is feeding us"?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, but I want to explain what it means. It means heaven forbid that you get into a position when the HVO is defending you and Caritas feeding you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, what about the bishop's premises? Was that destroyed by the Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was damaged. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The bishop had his seat in the cathedral; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And why were you so opposed to having the bishop stay at the house that the former mayor left to the town of Mostar? And I agree with you on that. And the bishop had no other place to conduct his religious services but the cathedral? And this house was owned by the town of Mostar. This house of Mujaga -- please remind me of the name.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Komandina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Komandina. So this was a socially owned house. I'm not going to explain all of this for the Trial Chamber now, but just tell me is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not fair of Mr. Topic at the time to give a house that was bequeathed to the town, and his son was still alive and the -- his last -- his will said that it should be returned to the Islamic community, and then to have it handed over to the Catholic church? And the Catholic church did have some premises of their own and the Islamic community didn't have any premises of their own, and he didn't take this into account at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, sir, distinguished witness, you are a man of learning. I ask you most kindly -- you hear my questions well. Please let us not dwell on this any longer. I asked you very kindly just to answer me whether this house was socially owned or not.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was socially owned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the bishop only spend three months there until his own office was repaired? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But he left this gentleman there at that house, and our forces found him there, and that is where he was left in order to open a bishop's Caritas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Didn't you get the entire students' dormitory, including the gym, where you could conduct your prayers?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it's better to put it this way: that we entered that students' dormitory. It's not that we were really given permission for that. So we tried to pre-empt the situation so that they would accept it as a fait accompli.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please be so kind, sir? Could we see the Prosecution exhibits from yesterday, please? The whole binder? Exhibit 739.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I think we are also entitled to be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. The usher is not wearing his headphones, and that's why I told him directly. Exhibit 739.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Have you found the version in Croatian, that is, the renaming of streets? Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My first question is the following: In which year were the streets renamed?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a report here from Slobodna Dalmacija, from Croatia. This is a report from 1995. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Precisely in that year, 1995. It's not a report. It's a decision of the municipal council that was published in all the media, in 1995, after Dayton. We had been living in a federation for almost two years by then. My second question --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm trying to say that this decision was reached in 1995. Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you know that these names of streets that were Muslim names were renamed and then started bearing the names of Croats? That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Distinguished witness, sir, please be so kind as to allow me to put questions. Listen to them carefully and please answer them.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that Rondo is a Muslim name, the square called Rondo? Please, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The Lenin Promenade, is that a Muslim name? Please, please. Is Lenin a Muslim name or not?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All right. But names were being changed -- please bear with me. Be patient.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you bear with me too. We cannot just go through this way. Rondo is a universal name. All the people of Mostar like this. So if they like it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber is certainly not expecting any debates among the Defence counsel and the witness. We have made a ruling that whenever this kind of argument happens, we will blame the counsel, rather than the witness, because you are conducting the cross-examination. Just be patient with the witness. You should understand that in the cross-examination, all the witnesses are somewhat hostile.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sir, Witness, Petar Drapsin, that was the name of a street that was changed. Is that also a Muslim name, Petar Drapsin?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you're talking about the core of the problem at all. I mentioned a few streets, and they are very well known, and they bore Muslim names. And many streets beforehand were named after Croats too, and now, why was not a single Muslim name left? That's the problem. The rest doesn't matter at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, the name of the street that was JNA, the Croat Vladimir Nazor, and the JNA was the aggressor, and then Matija Gubec, and then all the other names are from the communist period, will you agree that all of those names were changed?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a clear idea. Rondo is universally accepted by all. Why did the square, Rondo - that is very well known to the people of Mostar, wherever they would be - why was it renamed the Square of Great Croats? And all of this was done with the intention of having West Mostar as the town of Croats only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move on to another question. Could you please be so kind as to tell me whether Bishop Peric gave you this book as a gift? It's called, "For a Just Peace."

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was your entire correspondence published in that book, the correspondence between you and him?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was much later, after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I agree. It was published in 1995. But was your entire correspondence published in that book, the correspondence between you and the bishop?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of time has gone by. I can't remember all the details. But, yes, for the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we come across the same issues we had before. If you want to show some documents, you have to show this book to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that same point, I'm also concerned, frankly, that if there is some particular letter included in the book that he intends to use in any way, either today or in the future, to challenge this witness's credibility, it ought to be put to the witness. I fear -- I may be unjustified in this, but I fear there is something in that book that we'll hear about in the future that will not be put to the witness while he is here to respond to it. So I invite the Chamber to have counsel, if there is something in that book specifically to put to this witness, that it should be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, please, I kindly ask this Honourable Trial Chamber, I don't even say what I wish to say, and an objection is raised on the basis of something that I do not intend to do at all. The letter I'm going to talk about is a Prosecution exhibit. I just asked the witness whether this book exists and whether he received it. And this is Exhibit 467.2. Nothing else. Of course, nothing else occurred to me. We discussed this yesterday. I apologised today, and I said that I would never tender anything in the future if I do not have a sufficient number of copies in the English and the Croatian languages. And I just wanted to bring up Exhibit 467.2, which is a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, you may proceed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please look at the last page of this letter in the Croat language, because it's very long. If you wish, we can discuss the entire letter and your answer, of course; however, I would like to confine myself to Point 5(a), (b), (c). Point 5 begins as follows: "We are astonished, finally, Mr. Mufti, over some of the things that are contained in the book "Instructions to the Muslim Soldier", Zenica 1993, that was published by the office of the meshihat of the Islamic community of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 50.000 copies. "For instance, (a), chief characteristics of the devoutness of the Muslim soldier are that he goes to battle with the cry Bismilla in the name of Allah. Do you really want this to be a religious war?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to relevance, Your Honour. How is this an issue in the case or a defence to an issue in the case? I object to relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, have you explained what the relevance is for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course it's relevant, Mr. President, because it is quite contrary to all the allegations made by the Prosecutor in the indictment. Because this is the army of one party and of one faith and all the rest, the civil war, et cetera, et cetera. I have the indictment, of course, and of course my questions are based on the indictment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps Mr. Krsnik can take us to that part of the indictment to which this is relevant. He said, It is quite contrary to all the allegations made by the Prosecutor in the indictment. I have no idea what Mr. Krsnik is talking about -- or, again, I object to the relevance. There has been no showing whatsoever this is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you are aware of the general context of the indictment, and my client stands accused of that as well. Of course, the instructions to Muslim soldiers are not in this indictment, but this will be in the following indictment, and that is why the Prosecutor keeps opposing this by invoking the principle of tu quoque. However, in this case, this principle is not applicable, nor is that the Defence that we are trying to carry out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we understand the objections from the Prosecutor. But here we are not discussing the legal issues, especially on the principle of the tu quoque. We have received the submissions from the Prosecutor on these matters, but we regard it as just kind of reference material rather than some motions, and ask us to do anything on that issue. So we'll not spend much time on those issues. You may proceed with your cross-examination, but just bear in mind the objections from the Prosecutors on this point. We have spent a lot of time on this issue. We hope you could wind up your cross-examination as soon as possible. And now, it's 11.00. We have to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise. I do need to say, I believe, before the break, I am -- I can only say I'm very concerned about this witness being able to conclude his testimony before 1.00. And it would be a shame if he has to stay over the weekend again to testify for a few minutes on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can -- I can promise, Your Honours, that I will finish within half an hour, because I just have questions left that are related to mosques and everything that concerns mosques. And after that, I will conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just a brief comment: The documents that were supplied by our learned friends are here, and that was my first intention. I simply wanted to check them. Besides, we also have a reply to this letter. It is also in this binder. So that was the purpose of my questions. There. So with your permission, I'd like to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sir, do you have the text before you? You know, that item 5, the last page?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. Now, we are moving to item B. We've just been through (a). And again is the bishop writing to you, same letter, I mean? Did you find that? Item 5(a), (b), (c). Now, I'm reading (b). Or in these Instructions for the Muslim Soldier, it says: "Thus, for instance, if the superior officer or the higher command assess that in the interests of defence, protection of one's own people and superior goals, it is more proper to set fire to certain buildings, crops or forests, then it is permissible to do that because history teaches us that Mohamed, A.S., permitted the destruction of houses - of a house, excuse me, of a house - and felling of enemy palm groves in retaliation," page 25 of the Instructions for the Muslim Soldier. And finally, (c): "It is likewise left to the military command to decide whether it is more useful and of interest for the common cause to free, exchange or liquidate an enemy prisoner, page 26 of the Instructions for the Muslim Soldier, which is in glaring contradiction, especially the letter, with both the Geneva Convention on prisoners of war and common sense." And the letter is concluded with the following: "It is presumably in this context that one can interpret an occasional beret with the inscription, 'For Allah, against the cross.' We condemn that too. Praying to God to grant to us all a just and lasting peace as soon as possible. Respectfully yours. Ratko Peric." Did you receive that letter and read it?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to have your reply to that, Exhibit 476.1, last page of your letter, the second passage. Did you find it? Have you found that, the last page of your text, the second passage? And it says: "I marvel, dear Bishop, at your astonishment, as you put it, about the Instructions for the Muslim Soldier, since you know that Islam teaches that every good and noble undertaking, such as the defence of one's own life, defence of the people and homeland, and we have no other homeland except Bosnia and Herzegovina, begins with God's name." Now, if you want me to, if you want me to read the rest of it, but I'll ask you only questions about this particular passage. Now, do you want me to read the rest? I'm surprised that you do know. But what I'm interested is in his question and your answer. And this is how you answer -- how you reply to the bishop, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [no audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you then agree with me that these passages that the bishop quoted to you figure indeed in the Instructions to the Muslim Soldier?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I do not have the text with me, but I believe you. There is no reason to doubt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think in fairness to this issue, yesterday you very kindly furnished us with a translation of the "Instructions to the Muslim Soldier," which I read last night. With the greatest respect to the bishop and to you, the bishop has taken that particular passage out of context. Because reading this document yesterday, I was amazed at how many similarities there are in it to the Geneva Convention for the treatment of prisoners of war. And in fact, there is a paragraph here on page 24, which is entitled "Prisoners of War." And if I could read it out, because I think there must be some fairness in this. It says: "Prisoners of war are likewise the phenomenon inherent in every war. Islam has in this matter established firm rules which Muslim soldiers are duty-bound to follow. Although the foe in this war has gone beyond all measures in his crimes, Muslim soldiers are nevertheless bound by their faith to show justice and adhere to certain rules which apply even in wartime conditions. "To this effect, the killing of women, children, and priests who do not participate at all in the war --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpreters do not have a copy of this text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'll go more slowly. "... and who do not directly or indirectly assist the enemy is forbidden." And this is the important bit: "Likewise, it is forbidden to damage or destroy other people's sacred objects, cultural, and historical monuments. It is also forbidden to kill farm animals and to destroy crops and vegetation. Islam, likewise, forbids the torture and brutalisation of prisoners of war and the mutilation of enemy and continues very much in the line of the Geneva convention." It then goes on to say: "These are general rules which are binding for our soldiers; however, if the commanding officer assesses that the situation and the general interest demand a different course of action, then the soldiers are duty-bound to obey their commanding officer." Now we come to the piece that the bishop quoted: "For instance, if their officer or higher command assesses that it is in the interest of defence ..." So in other words, this is an exception to the general rule. So really, with the greatest of respect to the bishop, who I'm sure had his advisors, the little passage in his letter which you have quoted has been taken out of context, and I think you will agree with that. So in general, Islamic soldiers are forbidden to do what non-Islamic soldiers are also forbidden by the rules of warfare. And so really, this debate is not going to advance the case very much. There are no doubt soldiers on every side who either disregard the rule of Islam or disregard the Geneva Convention, and that's what we are dealing with. But I'm very glad that whoever furnished the Bench with this gave it to me because it made very interesting reading. But I really don't think the debate that you are conducting between yourselves at the moment is of interest. Obviously from a sociological point of view, it may be going a little bit outside of what we are here to face. This witness, as I reminded you yesterday, obviously has very strong views, and so do you. And they may not be the same views, but this witness has given evidence that there were 20 mosques before the war and there are now none. And really, you have to deal with that, if you think it relates to your client at all. This witness hasn't given evidence that he saw Mr. Tuta giving orders. But nevertheless, do you dispute that the 20 mosques were destroyed? And that's what we really have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour, for explanation and your views. Of course, I agree with them. I was not going to engage in a long debate. Merely in this chapter on the prisoners of war, which you have just read, it says that there are general rules which are binding on everybody. But then if somebody interprets it differently, then, it, of course, entails all the other consequences in these rules. But I will not ask any more questions. We heard the answer. I merely wanted to say why is the answer like that because all the clergy, all the men of God, should react and respond immediately, as soon as they see that something is in contravention of the teaching of God, of their religion and everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You also heard the instructions of the noble Judge, and we must go by them. So let us move on to the issue of mosques. And it is the last document which is in Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please, be so kind. My first question: Do you know as regards all the mosques that were destroyed -- mined - excuse me - or demolished in some other way, that one man was accused or, rather, one unit or specifically the unit called -- the man called Misic, and there is a case conducted against him in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Oh, you are not.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, the media wrote about that and covered it all. That's why I asked you. There is the trial before the higher court in Mostar -- I believe it is called "higher" because you do not have a district court. You are not aware that there is such a case before that Court?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Fine. But are you generally aware, do you have any knowledge, your personal knowledge, as to who destroyed them? -- you personally.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the individual or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, well, there are many mosques. I don't want to list them all. For instance, let's take the municipalities. Mostar North, for instance, municipality of Mostar North. You say the facilities which were destroyed or damaged by Croats. That is what I am going by, because naturally, what the Serbs destroyed, there is very extensive and exhaustive documentation. And we shall also be presenting this to this Court, needless to say. So I wanted to ask you, municipality of Mostar, Stari Grad, that's what I am asking you. I don't think we need maps, not to waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the old part -- the historical core of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about Hadi Mehmed [phoen], Kara Josa [phoen], and Ali Pasha's [phoen] Mosque? Are they also part of that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Then municipality South -- Mostar South, South Mostar, it is the penultimate -- no, it is the third page of your report, Mostar South. Is it outside Mostar, towards Rastani?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's south, so it's Buna, Grbovac, Pijesci, toward Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I see. And how far is it from the city of Mostar itself?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the present territorial subdivision, it also includes Jasenica and Rodoc, which are suburbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I see, suburbs, right. So tell me about Mostar, southwest municipalities. Is it again suburbs?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No. But that is in the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Oh, southwest?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mostar municipality, southwest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you mean the city?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I see. The city, yes. We are just trying to identify the locations. Then West Mostar municipality, there is only one meshdid [phoen] in the locality of Rastani, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That is another suburb. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you about southwest Mostar municipality, item 3. Three, isn't it? It says here -- to begin with, is it your signature or not? Because there is a signature on every page. Is that your page or somebody else's?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It says, "The mosque in the settlement of Balinovac," and that same individual called Misic has also -- is charged with the destruction of this mosque. But here we have an interesting sentence: "It was destroyed immediately after the outbreak of the conflict and there were several eye witnesses whom soldiers commanded by Tuta took to the Heliodrom camp." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: "And then those men, that is, the eye witnesses who were being escorted by these other men, saw the mosque being destroyed by a bulldozer and the stones being immediately taken away." What does Tuta have to do Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with that mosque? Why is his name here?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, men who returned from the camp said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That's fine, but why does his name come up here when he has nothing to do with this mosque, either he or his men? And I think it transpires from your text very clearly.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What transpires is that the mosque -- the mosque was mined on the 9th of May, on the day of the attack and the offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That's fine, but I'm reading your report. Tuta and those soldiers and the mosque have nothing to do. So why is it mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we established that there was a connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. Counsel has asked the question several times now and has still not given the witness an opportunity to provide an answer, and in addition to that, he several times made simple assertions that are contrary to what's in the statement. Now, my main objection is let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we believe that the witness should have an opportunity to answer the questions. And Mr. Krsnik, you conduct your questioning in such fast speeds, even we have some difficulties to follow you So rephrase your question, ask it one by one, slowly and clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My apologies, I shall read this once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It is item 3 of your report, the one that you wrote. And in this report, which you wrote, it says that "Soldiers commanded by Tuta took some men to the camp." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And then those men, that Tuta's soldiers --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that is what is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But it does not say so here.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that there is something which is missing from this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I see, something is missing. So what you are telling us today is correct, and the text that you wrote was deficient? I see. Right. Now, tell me the next thing, the municipality of Jablanica - it's the next page - "The mosque in -- at the locality of Sovici destroyed by explosives after the Bosniaks had been expelled." Now, was that a mosque or was it a meshdid [phoen] or was it a gazul hana? I've asked all the witnesses that, and I think you are the most competent person to ask of that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a mosque, a mosque with a gazul hana.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I see. So it was a mosque with a gazul hana?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you then be so kind and explain to the court what is a gazul hana?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the area where the deceased are dressed. Sometimes it makes part of the mosque; sometimes it stands on its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you tell me, please, was there a minaret -- did the mosque have a minaret?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I see. So the mosque in Sovici had the minaret?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it has the minaret -- if there is a mosque, at least that is how we understand it, and every mosque has a minaret.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you saw with your own eyes that mosque and that minaret?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, I went there to attend some services.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we move on to the item 2, item 2, the mosque and the settlement of Doljani. And there follows an interesting sentence: "It was set on fire and destroyed after the massacre." Will you tell me what massacre, who massacred whom, how many bodies, what date, and will you please tell us what you know about it?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, let me see, on the 17th, on the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How many people were massacred in Doljani?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number. I know that military were taken to a camp, that there was a very brutal attack on the village, that the villagers were imprisoned there, that they watched it, and some of them, that is, those who told me about that, were taken to Jablanica later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And on the basis of these stories of other people, you conjectured or you heard or something --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: -- that there was a massacre in Doljani?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And when was that mosque set on fire and destroyed? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some people stayed on for a few more days whilst they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But do you know approximately?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had no contact with Jablanica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. There are some indications that the units who did that under Naletilic -- were under the command of Naletilic. But that is something that you also heard from other people. That is also hearsay, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought this would be my last question but then my colleagues remind me that I have two questions more. But they are short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: First, could you give us the name of that anchor, of that host, in Split? You remember, the one that you testified about during the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you perhaps remember at least the month or the year of that programme, and then we can look it up at the HTV?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in May 1992. It could be the 17th or the 18th, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my final question -- and my final question, please: Is that certificate -- let me just find which exhibit is that. P168.1. [In English] Help me. [Interpretation] Please be so kind, does it say, "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna;" is that correct? Is that the school year 1991-1992?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did Yugoslavia exist at the time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Had -- was Croatia recognised in February 1992 and Bosnia-Herzegovina in late April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was somewhere there. I'm not -- I don't know the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And by that -- by those dates, they were components of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, weren't they? Is that correct? Until the date of recognition, they were components, they were constituent federal units, both Croatia and Bosnia, of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to check the dates. I'm not quite sure of that date in April when it was recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sir, what I want to know is to establish the school year 1991-1992. I'm asking you. No doubt neither Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina were recognised at the time. They were still an integral part of the federal state of Yugoslavia. Can you say something in this regard?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
