utterances.text: Very well. And my final question: The Croat Community Herceg-Bosna, was it created that very moment when President Alija Izetbegovic, following the attack on the village of Emo [phoen], said that it was not your war?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that statement of Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, efendi, and thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, during the direct examination by the Prosecutor, the witness did not mention my client at all as the immediate perpetrator of any of the acts mentioned, and the indictment does not refer to many of these things; so therefore the Defence of Vinko Naletilic -- of Vinko Martinovic does not have any questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, I would like to draw your attention to the destruction of those mosques in Mostar. In the southwest Mostar municipality, in his report, he said that the mosque was situated -- was under the control of Vinko Martinovic, Stela. Have you noticed that allegation in that report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. However, it is the Defence case, and we will prove it, that this mosque was not within the zone of responsibility of Vinko Martinovic, Stela. And we believe that this witness is not a good one to prove that. We are going to prove it through our own witnesses during our own case; so therefore there is no point that we take up your time, our colleagues' time, our own time, as a matter of fact. We have other documents, and this witness really cannot assist us at all in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a couple of questions. I do have one item that's not really my question so much, but I feel like I should point it out for the benefit of counsel for Naletilic. I'm informed that yesterday, there was a question to the witness during his cross-examination about some letter, I think a letter dated the 29th -- a letter or a meeting -- dated the 29th of April, 1993. I believe this was at page 60 of the transcript yesterday. And Mr. Krsnik put some question to the witness. And to be perfectly candid, I have not looked specifically in the transcript myself, but something about Mr. Demirovic saying that Mostar should be a glorious, Islamic city, or something to that effect. I am told that the English transcript gave the answer or interpreted the answer from Mr. Smajkic as saying "yes" to that question, and the French translation gave the answer as being "no". So if that's something that's important to Mr. Krsnik, I just thought I would point that out. If he wishes, he may seek to clarify that. I don't intend to go into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of the re-examination is to make clear what is not clear in the cross-examination. You have the full right to ask this witness about this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would be happy to, Your Honour. I am simply trying to assist counsel, but I will do it the way you suggest as well. Re-examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let's start with that, Mr. Smajkic. I don't know if you heard all of that or not. Do you recall a question yesterday, there was something about a meeting or a letter involving both you and Mr. Zijad Demirovic, perhaps others. And counsel for Mr. Naletilic pointed out some passage to you, said something about Mostar being a great or a glorious Islamic city. Do you remember that testimony, or that question?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the question. I have just heard now what the answer was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, I want you to have a chance to clarify what your position was on that. Did you agree with that, or did you hear that statement or, if you recall now, what your position was, in fact? Because the transcript apparently is not clear.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be sure whether we held this meeting. However, I know for sure what Mr. Demirovic's thinking is. He works on the protection of cultural monuments. And before the war and afterward, he worked on the protection of the cultural heritage of Mostar. And he is a great advocate of culture. I know Mr. Demirovic very well indeed, and I simply cannot believe that it ever crossed his mind to make the town of Mostar into some kind of an Islamic town. I talked to him about this often. This is the revitalisation of buildings and certainly the revitalisation of the image of Mostar. Mostar, that was an old town, it has a cultural heritage of over 500 years. And I believe that his line of thinking went along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. In connection with the questions that were put to you for some time about religious officers or officials that may have been associated with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, are you aware, sir, that it is the practice of perhaps most armies in the world to have officers and officials as such called "chaplains"?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you understand these officials -- and I use the correct term, and if I don't, forgive me -- someone like an emir, can you assist the Chamber, can you compare that person to what someone in a western army might be considered a chaplain?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it corresponds. It is an assistant commander for morale. I think that that is identical, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question. You were asked a series of questions about the Bosniak nation, whether there was a Bosniak nation. And there was a time in your testimony yesterday where that involved about what was recognised during the time of the communist regime and whether, in fact, the Bosniaks as a people were recognised by the communists. Now, I think that was one of those areas where you were not given the opportunity to give a full answer. Could you explain or take the opportunity, please, to explain to the Chamber how were the Bosniaks viewed by the communist regime. And I only ask that in relation to the questions put to you by counsel.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your intervention. I felt it necessary to talk about this question. However, because of the wish to be as short as possible and to save time, I decided to omit it, but it's a crucial question for Bosniaks. During the communist regime, Bosniaks were not recognised as an ethnic national group. They were recognised as "undecided." When I finished school, where I was supposed to put my ethnicity -- there was a particular entry that had to read that -- I had to put "undecided," whereas on the other hand, there were Serbs and Croats who were protected in an ethnic sense. Lately - that is to say, in the '70s, '80s, et cetera - there were intellectuals, Muslims -- let me remind you of another thing. In the '70s, they did make a step forward, the communist authorities. They provided a constitutional solution, legislative solution, that these undecided persons be called "Muslims." However, that is truly a wonder, because a Muslim is a person of a certain faith, in Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, wherever. However, they did not allow themselves to identify with the country where they lived. And that is why the Bosniaks kept making efforts in this direction. There was a critical mass of intellectuals who were preparing the ground for calling themselves by their present-day name. Muslims liked the idea of at least calling themselves Muslims rather than nothing, although they were not satisfied with this category or with this name. We are an autochthonymous [as interpreted] people. We have been here for centuries, et cetera. So now conditions have been created for us to participate on a footing of equality with the other peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina in creating our national awareness and carrying out our national programmes.

utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Clark would like to ask the witness some questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm availing of an opportunity which will never present itself to me again. I have the religious leader of the Islamic community in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm sure I'll never meet you again in ordinary life. I've also heard from the Prosecution that you are the last witness to deal with background. I want to tell you by way of background from the Court that we had a witness very early on in this trial who came from the town of Mostar but who is a protected witness and, therefore, I can't mention his name. And he was very helpful to the Court in background in dealing with the issues in Mostar from a civilian point of view. He was not a religious man, and he was not a military man. He dealt with what he considered to be the terrible tragedy of the destruction of the multi-ethnicity of the pre-war life of Mostar. Now, you are dealing with obviously a different side, although I don't think you differ in many ways. I want to have you, if you can, to clarify for me, the identity of the Bosniak nation. Now, you said that Mostar had a rich heritage, that it's 500 years old, and you mentioned that the Bosniak heritage, which was suppressed during the communist regime, was also 500 years old. And then you pointed out that you had -- you were there a long time. Now, can I ask you this: Was Mostar an important town at the time of the Ottoman Empire? Was it a Turkish town, an Ottoman town?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was an important cultural and commercial town during the Turkish rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Would it have been built, then, by the Turks? It would.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the core of the old city, these are all that remains of the Ottoman architecture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do the Bosniak people, then, descend from the original conquerors of this area? And there have been many conquerors, the Balkans and many wars going back a long time. But does the town of Mostar and the Bosniak people derive their ethnicity from the Ottoman empire?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are very few people who arrived on the wave of the Turkish conquest in Bosnia-Herzegovina and stayed there as Ottomans, as Turks. They were the government, the administration; whereas the rank and file people, people who lived in those lands also, unfortunately -- unfortunately, as it is happening again -- at that time, that population, the majority of that population were not recognised by the churches, by the eastern and western church. So when the Ottomans arrived, they embraced Islam in large numbers. So they are the autochthonymous [as interpreted] population, the native population, not the Turks who came to conquer and stayed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So what you are saying, they are predated even the Ottoman empire, but because of whatever differences -- so ethnically, they are totally different, and the religion has made them even more different?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, that brings me then - thank you - brings me to the mosques. Were many of these mosques very old mosques from the, obviously, the Ottoman empire?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no mosque in Mostar younger than 400 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I take it that they were -- that their continued existence was tolerated by the other national groups or ethnic groups who were in the area equally for centuries?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In other words, when the Ottoman empire fell, there wasn't a wholesale destruction of Ottoman culture in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Are you saying there were no modern mosques at all in the Mostar region and its environs, including the suburbs of Rodoc and so on?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You're nodding, and I think that means that you are agreeing with me, that there were no modern mosques built.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are some more recent mosques.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Were there any in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some suburbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, can you deal with the position of Catholic churches and orthodox churches. Were there any of those in the area of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the East Bank, there was no Catholic church. There was one in the west part of the church, the Franciscan convent and the cathedral church. In the settlement which is now called southeast municipality, there is a Catholic church which survived with minor damages, and there was no Muslim population there. But it has not been savaged. And in the northern part, there is another Catholic church, which during the conflicts between the Serbs and Croats and Bosniaks and Croats suffered considerable damage, and it is now being reconstructed. And that work is about to be finished. And there is a big orthodox church, the cathedral church on the East Bank, but that has been razed to the ground. And we are now trying -- if I can tell you that we are trying to provide the necessary conditions for the restoration of that orthodox church because it is the see of the orthodox archbishop. Now, because his residence was destroyed, because the Serbs left Mostar, he has neither -- all he has is just an ancient small church. He has no office or anything else. He is in Trebinje at present. And we'd like to make a breakthrough to somehow make an opening and enable the return of Bosniaks and also to achieve, by doing that, we would like to, in return, ensure the return of Bosniaks to Trebinje and the restoration of their religious objects there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Has there been any return to normality and mixture of multi-ethnic institutions in Mostar? In other words, do Bosniaks live on the West Bank, have Serbs come back?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the return is a process underway, albeit slow. However, we could say that of late -- rather, this year, there are a number of Serb returnees, people who have come back to Mostar, and the Bosniak population -- and that that population is concentrating in the west part of the city. However, the administration -- that is, people are coming back and communicating. But the administration, one could say Croat -- I have to say that the Croat is really persistent. They want to maintain, to sustain the division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I see. Now, returning to the videotape that we saw, and the documents that we read overnight, I read that the truth is a very important part of the code of Islam but that during wartime, one is permitted to tell an untruth. I think that's probably self-evident, probably. If you're going to be captured by the enemy, you are permitted not to spill the beans entirely. I accept that. But I take it that in the situation where you are talking to us, we are not at war. Did you genuinely not recognise that flag with the Arabic writing that was shown yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised it. Yes, I did recognise it. I feel there's some confusion here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I did not recognise the text on the flag. I did recognise the flag itself, but not the text. Today, the image was better, and I could recognise the text, too. It seemed that we had a better copy today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, in looking at it, I think all of us recognised the uniform of the mujahedin quite distinct from the Islamic interpretation of what a mujahedin is. You know what we are talking about. I also saw pietsi [phoen] and hodzas and various other disturbing elements, to say the least. I know that all the arguments, about that this was made long after the indictment. But do you know if those same people were involved in the conflict against the Croats in the early days of the conflict, before it broke into war between the Croats and the Muslims, or the Bosniaks, I should say.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: They were. You are uncomfortable with that, I take it.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like you to clarify. I think I missed something. So could you please clarify it for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I just wondered if you know, if those parties that I described in the video -- and I know the video was made in 1995 and the war was over. But if those same parties contributed soldiers, uniforms, money, assistance to the Muslim side, who were not at that stage called Bosniaks - I make a distinction - I should say the Muslim side, before the hostilities in 1993, and late 1992.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there were days the units did exist before but not in such uniforms and not with these insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Not with those internationally recognised emblems. And then finally, in relation to war and instructions for the Muslim fighter, do these instructions only apply when the faith of Islam is an issue in the war? If a soldier is a Muslim, he belongs to the Islamic faith, and he's fighting alongside other Muslims but the issue has nothing to do with Islam - it might be a boundary dispute or some such thing - are the same instructions given? Or are these confined to a war with a religious element?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am really glad that you put that question to me. I wanted to tell the gentleman, the Defence attorney, something on this subject. These rules that apply to commanders in the sense of their behaviour towards prisoners, that can be applied only in Muslim states where the shariat law is in force. So this is not binding on us in Bosnia at all. We haven't any shariat laws according to which these rules would have to be applied. I mean, there are commanders then, and there is a court-martial then, and then that court-martial would have to investigate, and then pass a verdict on liquidation -- I mean, that is not applicable in Bosnia. We recognise the civil laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... military law in time of war, so can I take it --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... applies only in country where shariat law is the dominant legal system, like in Saudi Arabia, and I think in parts of North Africa?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You've been really very helpful. I know I've gone way outside the scope of the indictment in this, but I will never get the opportunity to find out again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have passed the scheduled time, but I will ask the interpreter to give us a few minutes to finish with this witness today. Judge Diarra? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, I would also like to put a question to you in relation to the film. You are a very educated, religious person, so you could give me some very important clarifications. In Islam, in addition to traditional religious holidays like aid el kebir [phoen] or mud [phoen], any Muslim gathering has a spiritual aspect -- weddings, any kind of gatherings, funerals, et cetera. During these gatherings, when a religious official is called in, like yourself or an imam or a lower-ranking clergyman, what is the meaning of his presence at these gatherings? Can you explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I felt it necessary to refer to that event or that parade. That event was organised by the army. It was the general who the troops were parading for. I really wanted to say that, because on the basis of the pictures, I wouldn't want people to get the impression that we are some kind of military commanders who are very important in the sense of organising the army. We are not that. We were asked as authorities among the people to attend this festivity, as guests. It is only natural. This was the day of the corps or whatever it was, and of course, if the Mufti appeared there, he had to address the gathering. So that was my task in all. By your leave, by your leave, I would like to say quite openly - now, this pertains to military organisation more - as a man who belongs to a multi-ethnic community, who wants to live in that kind of a society, I don't like those cries. I say that as a religious leader. That is probably a consequence of everything that happened during the war. Everybody has certain emotions and they want to prove themselves in front of the people gathered there. However, there is no such unit any more. This is a wartime unit. There aren't any in such uniforms or with such banners, and everything has fitted into the framework prescribed by law. I do beg your pardon for interjecting this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This makes it possible for me to understand this properly. I read the definition of "jihad" in a dictionary, and it says there that that is the Muslim struggle for the promotion of positive values and that is in the face of negative values embodied by the devil and promoted by the devil. This interpretation that you gave is more esoteric. Your explanation is better. The problem is that we do not know why, before eating or even before entering these premises, there is a special word that is uttered by the Muslims, and we have understood that this had nothing to do with the fanatical context in which the words "jihad" and other words are put today. Could you clarify this for us now?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I mentioned five elements, approximately, and that's the definition of "jihad" in Arab terminology, and this is what is decidedly stated, that is to say the defence of the state, the defence of life, the defence of faith, the defence of property, and the defence of dignity and honour. These are the five things that a person struggles for. If any one of these five values is imperiled, then a man struggles against that, fights a jihad in order to have justice prevail. There is also the following interpretation. We can say that it has the connotation of Islam as well, and the name of God, or rather the present-day understanding of "jihad" is -- I mean, in the heads of people, is a rather confused and confusing one. However, the first point you made -- may I remind you of a sentence of Mohamed, who returned from a major battle, and he came to the people and said, "We came back." Fierce fighting was taking place there. People were losing their lives, et cetera, and he said, "We came from a small bottle. What awaits us now is a big battle." And these people were surprised and they asked him, "What kind of big battle is this now? And where we were and where our lives were threatened, that was a small battle, you say?" And then he said precisely what you said, "That is the jihad against oneself, the jihad within oneself, to fight for the positive, for the good, and to strike this kind of balance so that goodness would prevail among people and within people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much. You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for giving us your evidence. We all wish you good luck. Our special thanks will go to the interpreters and the court reporters for their cooperation for these proceedings. We are adjourned until 9.30 Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
